question: How does the opening verse of the prophecy define its thematic subject and identify its inspired author?
opt1: "The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite"
opt2: "The oracle concerning Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see in vision"
opt3: "The burden of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi the prophet"
opt4: "The lamentation over Assyria, revealed unto Zephaniah the son of Cushi"
correct: "The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite"
explanation: Nahum begins with the judicial oracle against Nineveh and identifies himself as the Elkoshite. Nahum 1:1 (KJV) - "The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite."

question: What solemn theological attributes regarding God's holy character and judicial retribution open the hymn of theophany in Nahum 1:2-3?
opt1: God is merciful to all empires, desiring not that any king should perish, but that all should pay tribute to Zion
opt2: God is jealous and revenges with fury against adversaries, yet is slow to anger, great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked
opt3: God is unsearchable in peace, overlooking national bloodshed when heathen cities offer gifts of frankincense
opt4: God is patient forever, reserving no wrath for idolatrous nations, but guiding their kings through gentle chastisements
correct: God is jealous and revenges with fury against adversaries, yet is slow to anger, great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked
explanation: Nahum portrays Yahweh as jealous, avenging, and slow to anger, but unyielding in justice toward the wicked. Nahum 1:2-3 (KJV) - "God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies. The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet."

question: What cosmic manifestations demonstrate the majesty and power of the LORD during His march of judgment in Nahum 1:3-5?
opt1: He rides upon four winged cherubim of brass, casts golden hailstones from heaven, and parts the Euphrates into dry paths
opt2: He commands solar eclipses across all lands, pours out sulfur upon the seaports, and shatters the cedar forests of Hermon
opt3: His way is in the whirlwind and storm, clouds are dust of His feet, He drieth up rivers, Bashan and Carmel languish, and mountains quake
opt4: He sends swarms of fiery serpents through the valleys, dissolves iron gates with lightning, and dries up the Persian gulf
correct: His way is in the whirlwind and storm, clouds are dust of His feet, He drieth up rivers, Bashan and Carmel languish, and mountains quake
explanation: Nature convulsively responds to Yahweh's presence as seas dry, mountains quake, and lush Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon languish. Nahum 1:3-5 (KJV) - "The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet. He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers: Bashan languisheth, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon languisheth. The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is burned at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein."

question: What searching double rhetorical question underscores the irresistible, consuming fury of divine judgment in Nahum 1:6?
opt1: "Who is like unto the LORD among the gods? who is glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?"
opt2: "Shall the prey be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captive delivered?"
opt3: "Who hath directed the Spirit of the LORD, or being his counsellor hath taught him?"
opt4: "Who can stand before his indignation? and who can abide in the fierceness of his anger? his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him"
correct: "Who can stand before his indignation? and who can abide in the fierceness of his anger? his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him"
explanation: No creature or fortress can withstand God's poured-out fury and rock-shattering anger. Nahum 1:6 (KJV) - "Who can stand before his indignation? and who can abide in the fierceness of his anger? his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him."

question: Amidst terrifying declarations of wrath, what foundational assurance of covenant grace is proclaimed in Nahum 1:7?
opt1: "The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him"
opt2: "The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe from all adversaries"
opt3: "The LORD will command his lovingkindness in the daytime, and in the night his song shall be with me"
opt4: "The mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him and remember his covenant"
correct: "The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him"
explanation: Nahum balances wrath against enemies with the goodness of God as a refuge for those trusting Him. Nahum 1:7 (KJV) - "The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him."

question: By what means will the LORD make an utter end of Nineveh, and what guarantee is given regarding the finality of the stroke in Nahum 1:9?
opt1: With consuming fire from the heavens He will burn her palaces, and her walls shall never be rebuilt
opt2: With an overrunning flood He will make an utter end, and affliction shall not rise up the second time
opt3: With seven years of severe famine He will destroy her people, and her crown shall be removed forever
opt4: With an army of fierce archers He will scatter her princes, and her memory shall be extinguished from the earth
correct: With an overrunning flood He will make an utter end, and affliction shall not rise up the second time
explanation: God promises Nineveh's destruction via an overrunning flood, declaring that affliction will not need a second blow. Nahum 1:8-9 (KJV) - "But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies. What do ye imagine against the LORD? he will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time."

question: What agricultural and behavioral metaphors illustrate the sudden, helpless destruction of Nineveh's conspirators in Nahum 1:10?
opt1: Like green grass scorched by the sirocco and chaff blown across desert sands, they shall vanish at twilight
opt2: As wild brambles entangled in the valley and wine poured upon hot stones, they shall be consumed in smoke
opt3: While folded together as thorns and drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry
opt4: Like withered fig leaves trampled under foot and broken pottery cast into the mire, they shall perish
correct: While folded together as thorns and drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry
explanation: The Assyrian elites, tangled like thorns and intoxicated, will burn like completely dry stubble. Nahum 1:10 (KJV) - "For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry."

question: What sinister figure who hatched plots against the LORD is described as having originated out of Nineveh in Nahum 1:11?
opt1: "A proud king of iron, that shed the blood of the righteous and defiled the temple vessels of Zion"
opt2: "A false prophet of Baal, that taught the kings of the earth to commit spiritual harlotry"
opt3: "An idolatrous conqueror, that blasphemed the God of heaven upon the battlements of Jerusalem"
opt4: "There is one come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the LORD, a wicked counsellor"
correct: "There is one come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the LORD, a wicked counsellor"
explanation: Assyria produced the 'wicked counsellor' (such as Sennacherib or Rabshakeh) who plotted against Yahweh. Nahum 1:11 (KJV) - "There is one come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the LORD, a wicked counsellor."

question: What comprehensive divine decree of extinction and degradation is pronounced against the Assyrian royal house in Nahum 1:14?
opt1: No more of thy name be sown, graven and molten images cut off from the house of thy gods, and "I will make thy grave; for thou art vile"
opt2: Thy palaces shall be given to foxes, thy royal scepter broken by foreign mercenaries, and thy body cast to vultures
opt3: Thy silver shrines shall be melted into tribute, thy princes blinded in chains, and thy capital submerged under salt
opt4: Thy royal lineage shall be sold into Egyptian slavery, thy gods cast into the river, and thy name blotted from memory
correct: No more of thy name be sown, graven and molten images cut off from the house of thy gods, and "I will make thy grave; for thou art vile"
explanation: God decrees the extinction of the royal dynasty, the destruction of idols, and prepares Assyria's grave because she is vile. Nahum 1:14 (KJV) - "And the LORD hath given a commandment concerning thee, that no more of thy name be sown: out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image: I will make thy grave; for thou art vile."

question: What joyous gospel proclamation arrives upon the mountains of Judah, and what are the covenant people summoned to do?
opt1: "Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly: for the day of the LORD cometh with healing in his wings"
opt2: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee; he is utterly cut off"
opt3: "Sing, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel; be glad and rejoice with all the heart: for the King of glory hath broken thy chains"
opt4: "Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee: keep holy Sabbath in all thy borders"
correct: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee; he is utterly cut off"
explanation: A messenger brings glad tidings that Assyria's yoke is broken, calling Judah to resume her festivals and perform vows. Nahum 1:15 (KJV) - "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee; he is utterly cut off."

question: With what urgent military commands is Nineveh sarcastically summoned to prepare for her impending assault in Nahum 2:1?
opt1: "The breaker of nations hath arrived at thy gates: sound the war trumpet, summon thy archers, and seal thy water cisterns"
opt2: "The hammer of the whole earth is drawn against thee: shut thy bronze doors, double thy watchmen, and gird thy swords"
opt3: "He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily"
opt4: "The devourer hath crossed the Tigris: sharpen thy spears, repair thy broken ramparts, and call upon thy gods for aid"
correct: "He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily"
explanation: The conqueror ('he that dasheth in pieces') advances, prompting ironical calls to fortify defenses. Nahum 2:1 (KJV) - "He that dasheth in pieces is come up before thy face: keep the munition, watch the way, make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily."

question: What divine restoration of His covenant people provides the theological backdrop for Nineveh's destruction in Nahum 2:2?
opt1: "Because the LORD hath remembered the tears of Zion, and hath gathered her scattered children from the ends of the earth"
opt2: "For the Holy One hath purposed to plant Israel upon her holy mountain, and foreign nations shall never spoil her harvest"
opt3: "For the Almighty hath broken the rod of the oppressor, that Judah may inherit the gates of all her adversaries in peace"
opt4: "For the LORD hath turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches"
correct: "For the LORD hath turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches"
explanation: God is restoring the majestic splendor of Jacob and Israel after Assyrian plunderers had ravaged their vine branches. Nahum 2:2 (KJV) - "For the LORD hath turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches."

question: What striking visual description portrays the elite invading army during the preparation for assault in Nahum 2:3?
opt1: The shield of his mighty men is made red, valiant men are in scarlet, chariots gleam with flaming torches, and fir trees are terribly shaken
opt2: Their helmets are of polished bronze, breastplates of iron, chariots rattle with iron scythes, and cedars crash down
opt3: Their banners are dyed in purple, archers clothed in blue silk, horses gallop like leopards, and desert sands rise up
opt4: Their spears are tipped with silver, shields inscribed with suns, battering rams plated in gold, and oaks uprooted
correct: The shield of his mighty men is made red, valiant men are in scarlet, chariots gleam with flaming torches, and fir trees are terribly shaken
explanation: The assault troops appear in terrifying scarlet and red shields, with chariots flashing like torches. Nahum 2:3 (KJV) - "The shield of his mighty men is made red, the valiant men are in scarlet: the chariots shall be with flaming torches in the day of his preparation, and the fir trees shall be terribly shaken."

question: How does Nahum describe the frantic, chaotic movement of chariots in the streets of Nineveh in Nahum 2:4?
opt1: They overturn market stalls, crush retreating infantry beneath heavy wheels, and sound like rolling thunder
opt2: They rage in the streets, jostle one another in the broad ways, seem like torches, and run like the lightnings
opt3: They assemble in ranks before the royal palace, fire blazing arrows into the clouds, and roar like desert whirlwinds
opt4: They charge against the stone battlements, shatter the iron bars of the gates, and gleam like morning stars
correct: They rage in the streets, jostle one another in the broad ways, seem like torches, and run like the lightnings
explanation: The chariots careen uncontrollably through the thoroughfares like flashing lightning. Nahum 2:4 (KJV) - "The chariots shall rage in the streets, they shall justle one against another in the broad ways: they shall seem like torches, they shall run like the lightnings."

question: What catastrophic breach of Nineveh's hydraulic fortifications brings about the immediate collapse of the royal palace in Nahum 2:6?
opt1: "The subterranean water tunnels shall be poisoned, and the foundations of the citadel shall sink into dust"
opt2: "The outer river walls shall be shattered by siege engines, and fire shall consume the king's treasury"
opt3: "The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved"
opt4: "The dams of the Tigris shall burst with an earthquake, and all the ivory halls shall be swept into the sea"
correct: "The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved"
explanation: The river sluices gave way, unleashing an overwhelming flood that literally dissolved the palace brickwork. Nahum 2:6 (KJV) - "The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved."

question: What mournful scene depicts the capture and exile of Huzzab (the queen or personified city) and her attendants in Nahum 2:7?
opt1: She shall be stripped of royal purple and led in iron fetters, while her maidens wail like cranes and sprinkle dust on heads
opt2: She shall be delivered into the hands of the Medes, while her handmaids walk barefoot through the snow weeping bitterly
opt3: She shall flee into the reed marshes of Babylon, while her palace servants sing funeral laments upon broken harps
opt4: She shall be led away captive and brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts
correct: She shall be led away captive and brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts
explanation: Huzzab is led into exile while her maids mourn with the plaintive cooing of doves, beating their breasts. Nahum 2:7 (KJV) - "And Huzzab shall be led away captive, she shall be brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts."

question: What cry of plunder encourages the invading forces to pillage Nineveh's inexhaustible imperial wealth in Nahum 2:9?
opt1: "Take ye the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold: for there is none end of the store and glory out of all the pleasant furniture"
opt2: "Plunder the royal arsenals, carry away the bronze chariots: for the treasures of Sennacherib are beyond measure"
opt3: "Gather the jewels of Ophir and the carved ivory of the kings: for her storehouses overflow with tribute of forty nations"
opt4: "Seize the golden shields and the purple vestments of the priests: for Nineveh hath stripped the whole earth for centuries"
correct: "Take ye the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold: for there is none end of the store and glory out of all the pleasant furniture"
explanation: The invaders are commanded to loot Nineveh's boundless hoard of silver, gold, and luxurious furnishings. Nahum 2:9 (KJV) - "Take ye the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold: for there is none end of the store and glory out of all the pleasant furniture."

question: What vivid triple alliteration and physiological manifestations of sheer terror portray Nineveh's complete desolation in Nahum 2:10?
opt1: "She is fallen, ruined, and burned: and their tongues cleave to their jaws, their eyes fail with weeping, and despair covers their souls"
opt2: "She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins, and the faces of them all gather blackness"
opt3: "She is broken, plundered, and forsaken: and their breath fails, their hands hang down limp, and darkness settles over their eyes"
opt4: "She is barren, silent, and desolate: and their bones tremble, their kings faint in dust, and bitter shame fills their palaces"
correct: "She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins, and the faces of them all gather blackness"
explanation: The famous Hebrew poetic triplet (bukhah, umbukhah, umebullaqah) is matched by trembling knees and blackening faces. Nahum 2:10 (KJV) - "She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins, and the faces of them all gather blackness."

question: With what predatory animal taunt does Nahum mock Nineveh's former imperial ferocity and relentless hoarding of prey in Nahum 2:11-12?
opt1: "Where are the swift leopards that leaped upon unsuspecting nations, filling their lairs with the bones of kings?"
opt2: "Where is the great dragon that lay in the midst of the waters, whose scales no iron spear could ever pierce?"
opt3: "Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions ... The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses"
opt4: "Where are the soaring eagles that built nests in the mountain crags, swooping down to devour the flocks of Judah?"
correct: "Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions ... The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses"
explanation: Assyria, which glorified lion hunts and rapacious plunder, is mocked as an emptied lion's den. Nahum 2:11-12 (KJV) - "Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions, where the lion, even the old lion, walked, and the lion's whelp, and none made them afraid? The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin."

question: What decisive divine confrontation and total silencing concludes Chapter 2 in Nahum 2:13?
opt1: "Behold, my hand is stretched out, saith the Holy One, and I will cast thy idols into the flames ... and thy royal name shall perish forever"
opt2: "Behold, I will summon all nations against thee, saith the LORD, and they shall sow thy citadel with salt ... and no king shall arise from thy seed"
opt3: "Behold, I have weighed thee in the balances, saith the Almighty, and found thee wanting ... and thy empire shall be divided among the Medes"
opt4: "Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword shall devour thy young lions ... and the voice of thy messengers shall no more be heard"
correct: "Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword shall devour thy young lions ... and the voice of thy messengers shall no more be heard"
explanation: God Himself stands against Nineveh, burning her chariots and silencing her intimidating royal ambassadors forever. Nahum 2:13 (KJV) - "Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword shall devour thy young lions: and I will cut off thy prey from the earth, and the voice of thy messengers shall no more be heard."

question: With what terrifying sensory description of carnage does Nahum introduce the woe against the 'bloody city' in Nahum 3:1-3?
opt1: Noise of a whip, rattling wheels, prancing horses, jumping chariots, bright swords, glittering spears, and a multitude of corpses with no end
opt2: Sound of a horn, shouting archers, roaring catapults, falling towers, rivers of burning pitch, and sulfur choking the streets
opt3: Crashing of bronze gates, marching legions, flashing shields, blazing arrows, weeping widows, and dust covering the dying
opt4: Thunder of siege engines, whistling slingstones, blaring trumpets, crumbling ramparts, and wolves devouring the slain
correct: Noise of a whip, rattling wheels, prancing horses, jumping chariots, bright swords, glittering spears, and a multitude of corpses with no end
explanation: Nahum provides an intensely cinematic auditory and visual portrayal of the cavalry and chariot onslaught filling the streets with corpses. Nahum 3:1-3 (KJV) - "Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery; the prey departeth not; The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the pransing horses, and of the jumping chariots. The horseman lifteth up both the bright sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of slain, and a great number of carcases; and there is none end of their corpses; they stumble upon their corpses:"

question: What spiritual and geopolitical abominations provoked this total ruin in Nahum 3:4?
opt1: The extortion of unfair trade taxes from the merchants of Tyre and the enslavement of peaceful Phoenician sailors
opt2: "The multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts"
opt3: The desecration of the sacred vessels of Jerusalem and the burning of the ancient law scrolls of Moses
opt4: The building of a colossal ziggurat to reach the clouds and the sacrifice of royal infants to the demon Pazuzu
correct: "The multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts"
explanation: Nineveh seduced, enslaved, and manipulated nations like a seductive harlot and sorceress through occult alliances and deceit. Nahum 3:4 (KJV) - "Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts."

question: What public humiliation and isolation will the LORD inflict upon the shameless capital in Nahum 3:5-7?
opt1: Burning her royal wardrobe, shaving the heads of her daughters, leading her nobles barefoot in chains to Egypt, with no ally to comfort her
opt2: Dismantling her golden idols in public view, dragging her priests through the mire, and banishing her queen into the desert of Arabia
opt3: Discovering her skirts upon her face, showing nations her nakedness, casting abominable filth upon her, making her a gazingstock with none to bemoan her
opt4: Smearing her city gates with bitumen, pulling down her stone monuments, and giving her ivory palaces as dens for desert jackals
correct: Discovering her skirts upon her face, showing nations her nakedness, casting abominable filth upon her, making her a gazingstock with none to bemoan her
explanation: God executes poetic justice on the arrogant city, exposing her shame like a degraded harlot made into an avoided spectacle. Nahum 3:5-7 (KJV) - "Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame. And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock. And it shall come to pass, that all they that look upon thee shall flee from thee, and say, Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her? whence shall I seek comforters for thee?"

question: What historic, seemingly impregnable Egyptian metropolis does Nahum cite as a cautionary precedent that fell despite infinite strength?
opt1: Memphis of the pyramids, whose defenders were as numerous as the sands of the Nile, yet was overturned by the kings of Persia
opt2: Babylon of the hanging gardens, whose bronze gates reached the skies, yet was dried up by Cyrus in a single night
opt3: Tyre of the rocky island, whose merchant navies dominated the Mediterranean, yet was submerged beneath the sea
opt4: Populous No (No-Amon / Thebes), whose rampart was the sea, yet was carried into captivity with her infants dashed in pieces and great men bound in chains
correct: Populous No (No-Amon / Thebes), whose rampart was the sea, yet was carried into captivity with her infants dashed in pieces and great men bound in chains
explanation: Nineveh had sacked Thebes (No-Amon) in 663 BC; Nahum reminds Nineveh that she is no more immune to destruction than Thebes was. Nahum 3:8-10 (KJV) - "Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea? Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers. Yet was she carried away, she went into captivity: her young children also were dashed in pieces at the top of all the streets: and they cast lots for her honourable men, and all her great men were bound in chains."

question: With what vivid horticultural metaphor does Nahum depict the effortless collapse of Nineveh's defensive strongholds in Nahum 3:12?
opt1: "All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater"
opt2: "All thy towers shall be like withered vines in autumn: if the wind blow, they shall be scattered across the desert"
opt3: "All thy fortresses shall be like brittle reeds beside the river: if an archer tread upon them, they shall snap in twain"
opt4: "All thy battlements shall be like dry wheat upon the threshing floor: if the fire touch them, they shall turn to ash"
correct: "All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater"
explanation: Her fortress walls will yield to the invaders as effortlessly as ripe figs falling directly into an open mouth when shaken. Nahum 3:12 (KJV) - "All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater."

question: How does Nahum describe the demoralization of Nineveh's garrison and the fate of her border defenses in Nahum 3:13?
opt1: Her soldiers flee like startled deer, her watchtowers are deserted by night, and foreign archers scale the unprotected walls
opt2: Her people in the midst are women, the gates of her land are set wide open unto enemies, and fire devours her bars
opt3: Her champions weep like motherless children, her iron swords melt like butter, and the waters of the Tigris flood her barracks
opt4: Her mercenaries mutiny against the royal guard, her city gates are opened from within, and foreign horsemen ride through unchallenged
correct: Her people in the midst are women, the gates of her land are set wide open unto enemies, and fire devours her bars
explanation: Assyria's once terrifying warriors become as powerless as defenseless women, and fire burns their gate bars. Nahum 3:13 (KJV) - "Behold, thy people in the midst of thee are women: the gates of thy land shall be set wide open unto thine enemies: the fire shall devour thy bars."

question: What futile emergency siege preparations is Nineveh mockingly told to execute, only to be devoured like what insect in Nahum 3:14-15?
opt1: Dig deep moats, erect iron palisades, and gather barley; yet pestilence and drought shall consume them like locusts
opt2: Cast bronze helmets, repair cracked parapets, and store honey; yet foreign archers shall strike them down like grasshoppers
opt3: Draw waters, fortify strong holds, tread mortar, and make strong the brickkiln; yet fire and sword shall devour them like the cankerworm
opt4: Hire Greek mercenaries, double the guard on the river dams; yet an overflowing flood shall drown them like crawling beetles
correct: Draw waters, fortify strong holds, tread mortar, and make strong the brickkiln; yet fire and sword shall devour them like the cankerworm
explanation: Even if they frantically make bricks to repair fortifications, fire and sword will consume them as ravenously as cankerworms. Nahum 3:14-15 (KJV) - "Draw thee waters for the siege, fortify thy strong holds: go into clay, and tread the morter, make strong the brickkiln. There shall the fire devour thee; the sword shall cut thee off, it shall eat thee up like the cankerworm: make thyself many as the cankerworm, make thyself many as the locusts."

question: How does the prophet describe the fleeting, unreliable nature of Nineveh's vast merchant class and military officials in Nahum 3:16-17?
opt1: Merchants richer than the kings of Tyre, princes clothed in gold who melt away like morning dew before noon
opt2: Traders like bees in a garden, generals boasting in bronze who scatter like dust before a mountain tempest
opt3: Brokers selling the plunder of empires, marshals commanding legions who vanish like smoke out of a chimney
opt4: Merchants multiplied above stars, crowned as locusts and captains as grasshoppers that camp in hedges on a cold day, but flee when the sun arises
correct: Merchants multiplied above stars, crowned as locusts and captains as grasshoppers that camp in hedges on a cold day, but flee when the sun arises
explanation: Nineveh's commercial and aristocratic hierarchy vanishes into thin air like numb grasshoppers flying away the moment the sun warms them. Nahum 3:16-17 (KJV) - "Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven: the cankerworm spoileth, and fleeth away. Thy crowned are as the locusts, and thy captains as the great grasshoppers, which camp in the hedges in the cold day, but when the sun ariseth they flee away, and their place is not known where they are."

question: With what pastoral lament addressed to the King of Assyria does Nahum expose the total collapse of leadership and scatter of the people in Nahum 3:18?
opt1: "Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell in the dust: thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them"
opt2: "Thy royal crown is fallen, O prince of Nineveh: thy captains are slain in the gate: thy children are carried into Babylon, and none can ransom them"
opt3: "Thy counselors are blinded, O monarch of the north: thy palaces are burned with sulfur: thy army is drowned in the river, and none mourneth"
opt4: "Thy wise men are confounded, O ruler of Ashur: thy seers are struck dumb: thy flock hath become meat to the beasts, and no shepherd defendeth them"
correct: "Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell in the dust: thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them"
explanation: The Assyrian rulers and generals ('shepherds') sleep in death while the scattered populace wanders the mountains without a leader. Nahum 3:18 (KJV) - "Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell in the dust: thy people is scattered upon the mountains, and no man gathereth them."

question: With what sobering declaration of an incurable wound and universal rejoicing among oppressed nations does the Book of Nahum conclude in verse 19?
opt1: "Thy days are ended, and thy throne is cast down into the pit: all kings shall walk over thy grave, for thy pride reached unto the heavens"
opt2: "There is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?"
opt3: "Thy judgment is sealed by the decree of the Almighty: the earth shall forget thy glory, for thou hast defiled the sanctuary of the living God"
opt4: "Behold, the sword of the LORD hath cut off thy root: and no branch shall ever sprout from thy stump, for thou hast hated righteousness"
correct: "There is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?"
explanation: The prophecy ends with an incurable fatal wound and universal hand-clapping over the demise of the empire whose cruelty touched everyone. Nahum 3:19 (KJV) - "There is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?"
